item.title: Adverse Childhood Experiences and the Hidden Cost of Growing Up in a Conflict-Free Home
item.description:
It may seem strange to say that quiet households aren’t necessarily healthy. Homes where there are no arguments between the parents, no slamming doors, and no visible discord are often depicted as the perfect home environment. But there are times that this perfect environment feels off. There’s an unnamed uneasiness, lingering in the shadows. Adverse childhood experiences aren’t just a product of loud and volatile environments.

These experiences often have roots embedded in homes where there was no conflict. In these homes, the silence itself has become the message. It’s important to pay attention to this as Scripture is clear about how to raise children:

“Train up a child in the way he should go, even when he is old he will not depart from it.” Proverbs 22:6, NASB 1995

Adverse Childhood Experiences in the Spaces Between the Words

Society commonly associates adverse childhood experiences with obvious harm such as abuse, neglect, or a household shaped by addiction or violence. But the definition reaches far beyond those familiar categories.

Other areas connected to adverse childhood experiences are emotional unavailability, chronically unresolved dynamics, or emotional environments that children absorb before they have a language to describe them. When conflict is permanently suppressed within a home, a different set of messages is sent.

Children are more perceptive than parents give them credit for. They notice when there is a proverbial elephant in the room that no one is talking about. The weight of unspoken disagreements and a cool distance between their parents are things that children can pick up on, even though no words have been spoken. What they see, and what they don’t see, is quietly shaping the way they understand the dynamics of relationships and how they should work.

When conflict is avoided, children often grow up believing that any form of disagreement is unsafe. This leaves them navigating adulthood without knowing how to have hard conversations in a way that doesn’t end in shutting down or walking away. This results in the lesson that conflict must be avoided at all costs rather than worked through. This is a lesson that most people do not recognize until adulthood.

How Adverse Childhood Experiences Shape Emotional Development

The emotional map that children use to navigate their feelings, relationships, and sense of self stems from the emotional landscape they grow up in. Christian counselors emphasize that individuals who present with anxiety, emotional avoidance, or difficulty sustaining a close relationship can trace those patterns back to early home environments.

These environments were not always chaotic, but they did lack emotional honesty. A conflict-free home doesn’t mean it is automatically healthy. The difference between these two types of homes matters in how a child’s emotional development happens.

Adults who were raised in households where healthy disagreement was never modeled often develop a heightened sensitivity to perceived social threats. These adults can read the room and learn to manage the emotions of those around them, quietly disappearing into whatever version of themselves fits the situation.

This leads to an internal fracture that masks a persistent, ongoing dilemma of not knowing whether their own feelings are acceptable. These adults spend many years managing others instead of realizing they have never learned to manage themselves. Emotional suppression in the home can give way to lasting difficulties in emotional regulation, self-worth, and relational intimacy. The soul will carry what the mind cannot yet fully process.

Faith, Healing, and the Permission to Feel

Scripture gives us a profound gift centered on the permission to feel emotions. The book of Psalms is a testament that God does not require positive feelings all the time. Grief, frustration, lament, and longing are woven throughout the biblical narrative from Genesis to Revelation. Adults who grapple with the residue of a childhood spent trying to understand emotional silence can understand the transformation of this biblical narrative.

God created us and does not demand that we hide our feelings; he invites them. He welcomes our open, honest feelings so He can comfort us and work in us.

Christian counselors understand that the healing process from early relational wounds is not a straight line. The adult will be required to learn how to identify emotions that were never given names or sit with discomfort that was once suppressed. They will need to understand how to rebuild a sense of what a safe connection feels and looks like.

These things can be found when faith serves as a foundation. This leads to confidence that God is present in the slow, hard process of becoming whole. This principle is the basis for genuine and lasting change.

The spiritual aspect of this process is significant in helping adults identify how they have internalized a distorted image of God as a result of growing up in conflict-avoidant homes. It removes the lens that says God is emotionally unavailable and requires composed compliance instead of a relationship. Scripture dismantles this image and offers one that says God draws near in the places we keep most guarded.

“Do not fear, for I am with you; Do not be afraid, for I am your God. I will strengthen you, I will also help you, I will also uphold you with My righteous right hand.” – Isaiah 41:10, NASB

Support for What You Could Not Name

One of the most complex dynamics adults experience is difficulty identifying what is wrong. They have no recollection of a dramatic event or of any identifiable wound. But they know that they have lingering effects in relationships and emotional availability.

They noticed that their sense of self was affected, and Christian counselors can provide the essential help needed to understand what happened. The result will be healing that is possible and worth pursuing.

When adults are willing to seek support, they are choosing to take an honest look at what they absorbed in childhood. It doesn’t mean they need to assign blame, but rather to bring the unnamed experiences into the light for addressing.

This will illuminate a connection between early emotional environments and their current relational patterns, allowing them to relax. They find they no longer need to maintain an impossible balancing act and can move forward with the healing that comes from naming the struggle.

Faith is a reminder that we are not required to carry these struggles alone. We were not designed to carry the burdens alone. Through community and honest conversations, we find that it is not weakness but rather reinforcement that will create a flourishing lifestyle based on the life that Scripture points to. We are reminded of God’s faithfulness to care for us in Psalm 147: “He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.” (Psalm 147:3, NASB)

Moving Toward Wholeness

It may not look like an issue that causes a struggle, but homes without healthy conflict create a specific kind of loss. It is a loss that goes unnamed and unknown for years. The face of a quiet adverse childhood experience is not easy to recognize, yet it is important to address. It is not an easy thing to name what happened in relation to adverse childhood experiences, but it is where everything shifts.

We don’t surprise God with our baggage. There is no distance from the layers of work that come with healing from what we absorbed before we could speak the words. Our journey toward wholeness doesn’t require having everything figured out. It only asks that we be willing to start and trust that we are not on the road alone. God is faithful to work things out for His good.

“And we know that God causes all things to work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called according to His purpose.” – Romans 8:28, NASB

Can you identify with any of this information? If so, please do not hesitate to contact the office and speak with the reception team. They can get you set up with an appointment to meet with the right counselor and start your journey to heal the wounds that have gone unnamed.

item.title: Finding Healing for the Wounds of Moral Trauma
item.description:
When you think of the word ‘trauma,’ what most likely comes to mind is something that’s been done to you or another person. That trauma could come from experiences such as acts of violence or even being caught up in a natural disaster.

There are other forms and sources of trauma, and they include the burden on your soul that results from spiritual and psychological distress. This moral trauma can strike at the heart of who you are, affecting your well-being.

Deep pain doesn’t just result from physical injury. At times, some of the deepest pains we carry are inflicted through other means. When your conscience and moral compass are violated, for instance, leaving you feeling disoriented, you may wonder whether you can be made whole again and if you can make your world make sense once more. Moral trauma, or moral injury, can be resolved, and you can find healing and transformation.

The Anatomy of Moral Trauma

Distress doesn’t only come from situations where you feel at risk or physically threatened. We are physical and spiritual beings. We can experience things that burden our souls and consciences, and that is where moral trauma resides.

Moral trauma, which is also sometimes referred to as moral injury, is the spiritual and psychological distress that arises when a person feels that they’ve violated their own moral or ethical beliefs.

Violation of your own beliefs strikes at the heart of who you are as a person; it can leave you feeling sullied, broken, confused, and in need of healing. When you feel betrayed by your own actions or inaction, or when others’ actions compromise you deeply, it’s a huge blow that strikes at who you are as a person. Often, the way toward healing will require new self-discovery and rebuilding what was lost.

Moral trauma differs somewhat from many forms of physical or emotional trauma. These often stem from a single life-threatening experience or event, while moral trauma can occur in those and other circumstances. When a person violates their own deeply held ethical or moral beliefs, or when they are put in a situation where they are powerless to stop such a violation, that can result in the distress that informs moral trauma.

When you’re traumatized by an assault, a natural disaster, or an accident, the typical result is that your fear response is triggered and becomes overstimulated. You may have nightmares, become hypervigilant, or engage in avoidance behaviors where you steer clear of the places, people, or situations that remind you of the incident. Moral trauma centers more on the loss of moral integrity, and it is rooted in shame, guilt, and the sense of spiritual disconnection one feels.

How and When Moral Trauma Occurs

In what sort of circumstances does moral trauma occur? The weight of moral trauma is rooted in what happened and what that means for one’s sense of right and wrong. The rupture of your personal and spiritual identity is a different sort of animal than the fear that gets unleashed by other forms of trauma and the reality of post-traumatic stress.

Moral trauma can occur in extraordinary situations where ethical dilemmas and human suffering intertwine, but it can also occur in everyday circumstances, too. Some of the contexts in which moral trauma may occur include situations where individuals may witness or participate in actions that conflict deeply with their moral compass, such as for those in law enforcement or the military.

This trauma may also result for individuals in healthcare or for first responders, where they make choices in life-or-death situations that feel ethically complicated or impossible to resolve. If you value life, making hard choices involving the lives of others can affect you deeply, and possibly lead to moral trauma.

In situations when you’re interacting or dealing with someone in a position of moral or spiritual authority, violations of trust, such as abuse or betrayal by such individuals, can be disorienting and traumatizing. It’s hard to reconcile your conception of the individual and their behavior, leading to a moment of crisis.

Lastly, moral trauma can also happen in everyday situations, such as moral compromise. This includes feeling complicit in wrongdoing by being silent or not doing anything about it. It can look like going along with a lie your boss tells at work or yielding to a bully by not intervening and protecting those who can’t protect themselves.

In these and other instances, what happens is an experience of deep inner turmoil that’s hard to reconcile. Witnessing or participating in something that violates your conscience or moral code can result in moral trauma, particularly if you don’t know how to process it or don’t have the support you need to work through it.

How Moral Trauma Can Affect You

While most other forms of trauma affect your fear response, moral trauma affects your spiritual well-being primarily, as well as impacts every other facet of your well-being. Spiritually and emotionally, moral trauma can leave you feeling far from the Lord, questioning your faith, and perhaps even being afraid of the Lord’s lack of favor or judgment. It’s a deeply upsetting and unsettling place to be.

Additionally, moral trauma can impact you by loading you with persistent guilt, anger, shame, and self-condemnation. As you remember what happened and try to make sense of it, you may be overwhelmed by these emotions and the feeling of failure.

Physically, moral trauma can result in disturbed sleep, ailments that are closely related to stress, like high blood pressure or stomach ulcers, and chronic fatigue. Mentally, you may experience difficulty concentrating on your tasks, as well as a sense of moral disorientation. The experience scrambles your sense of right and wrong as well as your place in the universe. You may also experience intrusive memories or unwanted flashbacks of the experience.

Last but not least, moral trauma also affects you relationally. As you try to make sense of things, you might find yourself withdrawing from loved ones, struggling to receive forgiveness or love from others, and you might also distrust others and yourself as well. At a time when you need others most, moral trauma can draw you toward isolation, which makes things more difficult. However – thank the Lord – there are pathways to healing from moral trauma.

Finding Healing for the Wounds of Moral Trauma

Even when you feel like you’ve let yourself, the Lord, and others down, life still has meaning, and it can be full of joy once again. We are all broken, and we act inconsistently and out of alignment with our deepest beliefs. The path of discipleship and following Jesus is about learning and growing to become the people we already are, by grace, in Him. In Christ, our brokenness and broken stories can be redeemed.

It’s hard to shake the shadow of moral compromise and the weight of trauma that it can load upon our shoulders. It is possible to surrender guilt and shame, embracing forgiveness and the wholeness that Jesus brings (John 10:10). Whatever you’ve experienced or done doesn’t have to control or shape the rest of your life. Some life-giving steps you can take include:

Acknowledgment and Confession Light is an amazing disinfectant, and that applies to our moral wrongdoings as well. Bring the hurt, inconsistency, guilt, and failure into the open. Psalm 51 is an amazingly honest reflection on moral failings that can result in moral trauma, and it can set the pattern for your own reflections, acknowledgment, and confession before the Lord.

Reframe Things The disorientation you experience from moral trauma can be counteracted by grounding yourself again in the truths of God’s word. There, you encounter truth bound up with grace, mercy, and forgiveness, which can help you reframe what you experienced. Consider and reflect on John 8:1-11; John 21:15-19; 1 Timothy 1:15-17; and Romans 8.

Acts of Service Guilt can be transformed into growth and purpose when you engage in acts of service or seek reconciliation where appropriate. It’s not so much that you’re making up for anything, because in Christ our debt is paid in full (Colossians 2:6-15), but it’s leaning into and living according to your purpose in Him.

Seek a Safe Community and Counsel Our lives aren’t meant to be lived in isolation, even in those moments when we are struggling to endure our own company. Share your story with others like a trusted and wise friend, a spiritual advisor, or a professional Christian counselor. This is an important step in dismantling the isolation that moral trauma often creates.

You can find help from a professional Christian counselor who uses trauma-informed therapy and faith-based resources to help you find healing and hope. Reach out today to connect with someone who can help you overcome the wounds of moral trauma.

item.title: How Play Therapy Helps Preschoolers Navigate Big Emotions
item.description:
Preschoolers are young children who live in a world where emotions are often bigger than words can contain. Their scraped knee becomes a catastrophe, and sharing a toy feels impossible. As preschoolers move from one activity to another throughout the day, there is always room for meltdowns. To us, these seem disproportionate to the situation, but the important truth is that these children are experiencing genuine distress.

The challenge is a preschooler’s lack of language and cognitive tools to express their feelings. Play therapy is the bridge between a child’s inner world and their ability to process big and difficult emotions. It meets them in their natural language of play. When preschoolers cannot tell you what happened, they will feel more comfortable showing the event through their play. This form of expression is their voice when words fail them.

As parents, we know it is important to teach our children. Scripture emphasizes this:

Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it. – Proverbs 22:6, NIV

Understanding the Developmental Stage of Preschoolers

The preschool years are typically ages 3-5, and they represent a period of rapid brain development. In this stage, children are learning to separate from caregivers, assert their independence, and navigate social relationships with other preschoolers. The part of the brain that is responsible for emotional regulation and executive function is still developing. This results in a gap between what they feel and what they can manage.

Preschoolers experience the full intensity of emotions without the capacity to regulate them. When a child is anxious about starting preschool or frustrated when a block tower falls, these emotions are as real and overwhelming as any that adults may experience. The difference between their experience and that of an adult lies in their ability to name, understand, and cope with these feelings.

Traditional talk therapy, which is typically used in these situations, often poses challenges for preschoolers. At this age, children do not have the developmental capacity to have a sit-down discussion about their feelings in abstract terms.

A three-year-old who is struggling with separation anxiety cannot explain the fear that grips them when they watch their parent leave or the tightness in their chest that results from that fear. When a four-year-old sees a frightening event, they may not have the vocabulary to describe what they saw and how it made them feel. Their developmental stage has not given them the tools or skills to navigate these situations.

While they are young, and these may seem like small things, we are reminded that even small things have great value:

Do not despise these small beginnings, for the Lord rejoices to see the work begin. – Zechariah 4:10, NIV

How Play Therapy Works for Preschoolers

The process of play therapy is a simple yet profound principle that allows children to express themselves through play naturally. Christian counselors create safe, structured environments for children to explore emotions through toys, art, materials, trays, puppets, or storytelling.

Each of these becomes a communication tool for a child struggling with situations such as witnessing a frightening event or sibling rivalry. The playroom itself becomes a sacred place where feelings that have been locked up can find room to escape and bring healing.

The counselor observes the patterns the child uses during play and notes recurring themes, shifts in energy, and moments when the child may seem stuck. Christian counselors, trained in this type of treatment, understand that the child takes the lead. The counselor offers general reflections, creating space for the child to work through the experience at their own pace.

The child can externalize what feels overwhelming internally. When they use a toy to express anger, they learn that anger can be acknowledged, contained, and managed. With the right guidance, the child is permitted to explore the feeling without judgment.

The Role of Play Therapy in Emotional Processing

Play helps young children make sense of the world. They rehearse social scenarios, experiment with cause-and-effect, and develop problem-solving skills. Play becomes more essential when emotional challenges arise. Children who have experienced trauma, witnessed conflict, or struggled with anxiety often carry these experiences in their body and behavior without conscious awareness.

It is well known that young children process experiences through repetition. Their behaviors are not random. Play therapy provides a safe environment for natural processing to occur with professional guidance. This allows the child to navigate big feelings about experiences such as a frightening car ride or family disruption. Each session will build on the previous one, which creates a pathway toward emotional understanding and resiliency.

A child may repeatedly crash toy cars together as they work through the memory of an accident. Another child might use dolls to recreate a scene from home, trying to understand what happened between their parents. This repetition is not a meaningless activity. It represents the child’s attempt to gain control over an experience that felt chaotic and uncontrollable.

Some Christian counselors specialize in child development and can help with healing the whole person through play therapy. For Christian families, play therapy with Christian counselors can include prayer and biblical stories adapted to the child’s level. This integration respects the child’s developmental stage while honoring the family’s faith values.

When Christian Counselors Recommend Play Therapy

Many situations lead families to seek play therapy for preschoolers. Behavioral challenges that persist despite consistent parenting often indicate that a child is struggling with something beyond typical developmental phases. Signs of these challenges are aggression, withdrawal, excessive fears, or difficulty with transitions.

When family structure changes, preschoolers can be overwhelmed, and their coping capacity is diminished. Exposure to traumatic events, medical procedures, or ongoing stress may warrant professional support and play therapy.

Christian counselors who work with these young children assess the presenting behaviors as well as the family context and support system. These counselors are looking for patterns that suggest a child is carrying emotional weight without the tools to release it. Some parents may describe a child who was previously joyful becoming withdrawn, or a typically flexible child becoming rigid in controlling.

These types of shifts signal that something has disrupted the child’s sense of safety or predictability. The goal is to understand what the behavior is communicating about their inner experience.

Play therapy often becomes the chosen form of treatment after multiple approaches have been tried. Parents decide after they have implemented all the tools they have, and they still face challenges with their preschooler.

This is not an indication of any failure, but rather a recognition that some emotional needs require specialized support. Christian counselors can help these families with compassion. This helps the parent understand that choosing help demonstrates strength and commitment to their child’s well-being.

Is play therapy right for your child?

The preschool years are an important foundation for how children will understand and manage emotions throughout their lives. When these young children receive support during times of distress, they will learn that feelings are manageable and that help is available. Play therapy offers a developmentally appropriate pathway for preschoolers to process the big emotions that words cannot capture.

Christian counselors are available to families seeking to integrate faith with therapeutic practices. When children learn that they are loved by God, known by name, and valued beyond measure, they carry a truth, even though they may not articulate it. Play therapy is a technique that honors the dignity and emotional needs of the tiny humans among us.

If your preschooler is showing signs of emotional distress, contact our reception team to learn more about how play therapy can support your family’s journey toward healing and hope. Our office can connect you with a Christian counselor who specializes in early childhood mental health.

item.title: Anticipatory Grief: Living With Grief Before the Loss Arrives
item.description:
There are times when grief may be experienced before there is even a loss. These forms of grief settle quietly, often long before a diagnosis is confirmed or before a loved one draws their final breath.

This experience is called anticipatory grief. It is going through the process of mourning for a loss that has not yet happened. For many, it often feels heavier than the grief that will immediately follow the death.

These are emotions that surface during this time; they are real and layered. These emotions are also misunderstood by the person living through them and those watching from a distance. This kind of sorrow deserves to be named, witnessed, and held with gentleness, just like any other form of grief.

The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit. – Psalm 34:18, ESV

What Anticipatory Grief Actually Means

There is no protocol or script for anticipatory grief. There is no checklist of emotions to move through or a predictable sequence to follow while navigating this type of loss. It arrives in waves. There may be an experience of acceptance, followed by a surge of fear or a brief period of peace disrupted by the heaviness that comes from nowhere.

These emotions could surface when someone receives a terminal diagnosis, when an individual declines due to dementia, or during an anticipated ending, such as a relationship. This type of loss is still on the horizon, but the heart has already begun preparing for it in ways. The mind has not yet become ready to acknowledge it.

The difficult aspect of this experience is the ambiguity it brings. The individual or the relationship is still present, and there are good days with laughter and shared meals that make it seem as though everything might be okay. But beneath it is a quiet current of awareness that suggests this season of life may be coming to an end.

Christian counselors understand that anticipatory grief is legitimate, and it is a deep human response that deserves thoughtful support and honest acknowledgment.

Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me. – Psalm 23:4, ESV

The Emotional Weight of Grief and What It Carries

Anticipatory grief comes with a disorienting aspect of the many emotions it holds at once. There is sadness and anger. This anger is at the situation, the unfairness of it, and for some, at God. Guilt is present because the process of mourning has already begun, and the person is still alive.

Exhaustion creeps in from holding space for the present and the fear of the future simultaneously. Along with these, there is a deep loneliness that stems from the inability to name or explain to those who have not experienced it. This can take place even when others are present.

Regardless of what culture may say, emotions are not a sign of weakness or a lack of faith. If you read the Psalms, you will find raw, honest lament as men and women cry out to God in the middle of circumstances they could not change or control.

This same honesty is available to anyone who is navigating anticipatory loss. This process carries an emotional charge that is real and calls for compassion, not correction.

When people move through this season, they feel pressured to stay strong for the person who is ill or other family members watching. But this pressure can push grief underground, where it becomes far harder to process and much harder to release over time.

Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God. – Psalm 42:11, ESV

Faith as an Anchor in Anticipatory Loss

Christians who struggle with anticipatory loss often experience a particular kind of spiritual wrestling. In the prayers of healing, there is an awareness that healing may not arrive in the form being hoped for. There is a deep love for a God who is sovereign and good, set beside an honest ache at what that sovereignty seems to allow.

This is not a failure of faith, but honest faith about what it does and doesn’t understand. It is this honesty that draws us closer to God as He meets us where we are.

We are not asked in God’s word to pretend that sorrow does not exist as a season to pass through quickly. We read where Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus, even though He knew it was about to happen. Grieving while holding hope is not inconsistent. It is the embodiment of what it means to be human before a God who is present in sorrow.

Christian counselors are trained to walk beside those who experience this spiritual and emotional complexity. They are available to help these individuals hold both the faith and their pain without being asked to choose between them or diminish what they are genuinely feeling.

He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away. – Revelation 21:4, ESV

Finding Support as You Navigate Grief and Uncertainty

Navigating anticipatory grief without support is not what God intended for His children. Many people try because they don’t want to become a burden to others, or because they are uncertain whether their sorrow is valid before the loss occurs. It is important to find a support system during the season and understand that it will look different for everyone.

Still, it will include trusted relationships and permitting others to show up in practical ways. Individuals who do not know where to look for guidance should understand that professional help will assist them in carrying the weight during the season of uncertainty.

Journaling, prayer, and taking time for intentional rest are anchors that can be a great benefit during this time. It is not selfish to be present for the person who is ill and allow yourself space to grieve.

This is necessary for a person’s long-term emotional and spiritual well-being. Christian counselors are available to help individuals and families identify what they need to communicate about grief and to hold space for both sorrow and sacredness.

Cast your burden on the Lord, and he will sustain you; he will never permit the righteous to be moved. – Psalm 55:22, ESV

Facing the Grief

Anticipatory grief is not an indication that something has gone wrong in a person’s heart or faith. However, it is a sign that love is deep, and the coming loss is real. God does not ask anyone to face this season in isolation, as it is one of the most human experiences a person can face.

Sorrow, fear, and exhaustion are not obstacles to faith. These emotions are invitations to bring what is true to God, who already knows. This is where healing begins. It is the willingness to be honest about the weight, to open the way to community, to professional care, and to a God who will draw near to the brokenhearted.

If you have been facing anticipatory grief and the weight that lies ahead, you do not have to navigate this journey alone. You can contact our reception team to connect with someone who can support your faith and mental health. Some professionals are willing to walk beside you as you navigate the uncertainty of this season.

For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. – Romans 8:38–39, ESV

item.title: Overcoming Grief with the Help of a Christian Grief Counselor
item.description:
Typically, the question of whether grief counseling is for you is reserved for the end of these types of articles. It comes after describing what grief counseling is, the role of a grief counselor, the pros and cons of grief counseling, and exploring group versus individual grief counseling. Still, it can be helpful to address this question up front. Will a grief counselor help you process your loss?

Signs of Grief

If you find yourself struggling to cope with your emotions in the wake of loss, that suggests that counseling could be a helpful next step. Some signs that indicate you could benefit from grief counseling would include the following:

Sleep Issues Having trouble falling and staying asleep, or you find yourself oversleeping

Changes in Appetite Experiencing changes in your appetite, such as not eating much or eating way more than you usually do

Avoidance Avoiding people, activities, or the places that remind you of what you’ve lost

Physical Symptoms Fatigue, headaches, or gastrointestinal issues that aren’t resolved using regular remedies

Feeling overwhelmed and experiencing persistent feelings of guilt, anger, sadness, or even numbness can indicate that you’re struggling with grief. This is especially true if these feelings make it hard to carry on as usual with your life. Struggling to cope in this way may indicate a need for counseling.

Lastly, if you’re turning to substance abuse, risky behaviors, or other unhealthy coping mechanisms, help is key. These can include food, work, or indulging your anger, which could indicate that you could benefit from time with a grief counselor.

Some or all of these might sound familiar to you. It’s important to take loss seriously and to consider how you’re responding to that loss. Grief can take you to dark places. Talking with a grief counselor can provide you with the space you need to work through your emotions and experiences, as well as nurture healthy coping strategies to deal with the loss without harming yourself in the process.

Obstacles to Reaching Out to a Grief Counselor

If you’ve experienced loss and you’re grieving, it’s quite likely that someone has brought up the idea of seeing a counselor. There are many good reasons to see a grief counselor, but it’s important to address the objections, stated or otherwise, that might make it hard to pick up your phone or send a message to a counselor to set up a session.

Each person has their own struggles and ways of processing things. There’s a verse in Scripture that says, “Each heart knows its own bitterness, and no one else can share its joy.” (Proverbs 14.10, NIV) It’s never wise to presume, but some common obstacles stand in the way of reaching out for help, even when it is sorely needed.

One obstacle is that if you and everyone around you see you as the strong one, and you feel you need to hold it together for them and for yourself, it can be tough to take that courageous step of asking for help. If you’re always strong for others, it can be hard to trust others with yourself and your vulnerabilities. You might even be afraid of losing control or of being overwhelmed by your emotions once you let them out.

Another possible obstacle is social or cultural barriers that make it awkward to ask for help. It might be uncomfortable to talk about family business with outsiders. Seeking help from others might be strongly discouraged because it could be embarrassing for the family. Such pressures make it hard to seek professional help. Find a counselor who’s culturally sensitive to your situation can also be challenging.

Much has happened in the last few decades to remove the stigma and misconceptions about counseling. That doesn’t mean such ideas have been completely erased. There are still some who view talking with someone about feelings and experiences as vulnerable or weak. This, combined with misconceptions about what counseling is and how it works, can all conspire to prevent someone from seeking the help they need.

Grief counseling could be hard for someone because of the possibility of feeling overwhelmed when talking through various life experiences. Grief brings up all sorts of memories and feelings, and not all of them are pleasant or easy to handle. The thought of confronting painful emotions or memories can cause deep anxiety.

Lastly, there may be practical barriers that stand in the way of seeking counseling for grief. Perhaps there are concerns about how much it will cost, whether insurance will cover it, access to quality counseling services in your area, or mundane concerns like finding the time to schedule appointments. All of these are valid concerns, but it’s important to weigh the benefits of seeing a grief counselor against these obstacles.

The Benefits of a Grief Counselor. Helping You Navigate Your Grief

Grief can enter your life in various ways, just like loss makes itself felt in different ways. Our loved ones die, sometimes suddenly, but also when we expect it after a long illness. Cherished relationships end, whether through mutual agreement or with bitterness. Long-held dreams, communities and places that have shaped and nurtured us, and work that gives us meaning, can all be lost, resulting in grief.

Grief is a necessary process for us to begin finding our way in the world again after experiencing loss. It’s the way to make sense of life as it is now, and to try and find the road to a full life. It’s not an easy road, as it is strewn with complex and difficult emotions. We don’t always know how to navigate through it all.

At the heart of it, the primary value and benefit of a grief counselor is that they provide you with a structured, non-judgmental, compassionate, and safe environment to work through the complex emotions that loss creates in our lives. Your counselor is there to help guide you and provide you with practical ways to cope with the pain, confusion, uncertainty, and challenges that come with loss.

Grief counselors are there to help you find your way back toward yourself in this new season of life, to find healing and a way to flourish in a new reality where things have changed irrevocably. These are some of the benefits of a grief counselor walking alongside you.

Navigating Grief’s Emotions Your counselor provides you with emotional support by validating your emotions. They can remind you about what grief is like, that it has no set timelines, that it will bring emotions like anger, sadness, relief, or guilt with it, and that these are all normal. Your counselor provides you with a place to connect and freely express your thoughts and emotions.

Exploring Tools for Healing Your counselor can also equip you with effective tools and techniques to make sense of your loss and grow through the process. Your counselor may teach you practical coping strategies such as journaling, mindfulness, breathing exercises, and other practical tools to help manage the sometimes-overwhelming emotions that come with grief.

While it can be hard, your counselor can also help you process the loss by exploring your relationship with your loved one, the circumstances of the loss, and what it all means for you. Part of the process is coming to terms with the reality of the loss. This involves integrating that loss into your current reality so that you can learn to live well in the wake of grief.

Replanting and Rebuilding A grief counselor can also help you find ways to not only honor your loved one and your relationship, but to rediscover meaning, purpose, and identity after the loss. Finding a renewed sense of purpose, connecting deeply with the Lord, and making the necessary life transitions are all part of the healing process.

Your counselor can help you to adjust and navigate new roles and circumstances that the loss thrusts you into. Walking alongside you, your counselor can help you nurture long-term emotional resilience, enabling you to handle future challenges.

Grief counseling is a helpful tool to use when you want to work your way through loss in a way that helps you rebuild and go on with life. Through honest, vulnerable conversations, setting clear goals and expectations with your counselor, engaging in counseling, and allowing yourself the time you need to heal, you find a way to live well.

If you’ve experienced loss, it affects you in small, imperceptible ways as well as large, obvious ones. With the help of a grief counselor, it’s possible to work through the grief, honor your loved one, and learn to live life in changed circumstances. Don’t hesitate to reach out to a grief counselor for help navigating the emotions and experiences stemming from loss.

item.title: Managing Stress When Living With Chronic Illness
item.description:
Chronic illnesses often come with a weight that others cannot see. Doctors’ appointments are routine, and medications are lined up on the counter. The good days and the bad days have blurred into a pattern that you never intended for your life.

Beneath it all runs a current of stress that doesn’t take a break when you need it most. Managing stress has become another task on a list that already feels impossible, and ignoring it only creates more physical symptoms to battle.

The challenge of living with chronic illness goes beyond learning to cope. This task involves recognizing how deeply connected stress and chronic illness are as they feed each other and create a cycle that feels unbearable. With the proper support and perspective, people who live with chronic illnesses can learn to interrupt this cycle and create a different reality. There is hope of finding genuine peace, even when their bodies refuse to cooperate.

Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. – Matthew 11:28, NIV

When Your Body Becomes the Source of Daily Uncertainty

Most of the time, healthy people can predict what their bodies will do tomorrow. They can make plans without wondering whether their energy will show up, and they don’t have to count the cost of every activity in terms of pain or fatigue. But those with chronic illnesses do not have the luxury of this predictability. Your body becomes unreliable, and that uncertainty creates a specific type of stress that others do not understand.

Some days you may wake up feeling capable, but by the end of the day, you’re barely able to function. The unpredictability affects everything you do, including work, relationships, and your sense of self. This isn’t about a weakness or poor planning; it’s about living in a body that doesn’t conform to the health expectations people often take for granted.

The stress of this uncertainty often makes you feel worse than the physical symptoms themselves. Before long, you find yourself making decisions based on worst-case scenarios. For instance, you decline invitations because you can’t guarantee you’ll feel well enough, and you overcompensate on good days, trying to accomplish everything before your body shuts down again.

Christian counselors recognize this pattern and help you develop flexibility rather than rigid control. They understand the goal is not to eliminate uncertainty, because doing so with chronic illness is impossible. They seek to help you learn to make peace with not knowing and plan wisely while releasing the illusion of complete control.

The Lord is my strength and my shield; my heart trusts in him, and he helps me. – Psalm 28:7a, NIV

The Hidden Burden of Managing Stress with Chronic Illness

Stress and chronic illness have a relationship that runs in both directions. Stress is not a result of being sick, but it does worsen some symptoms. Psychological stress can trigger inflammation, suppress immune function, and intensify pain perception. For those with an autoimmune disease, a stressful week may mean they experience a flare-up for days. Those with chronic pain struggle with the added emotional strain of carrying unbearable pain.

The body and mind are not a separate system. They are deeply interconnected, which means managing stress isn’t optional self-care. Because managing stress is essential, this creates another layer of pressure as you try to reduce it while dealing with an inherently stressful situation. You try to follow the advice to rest and stay positive, but you worry about falling behind, which leaves you discouraged.

Many individuals with chronic illness often face judgment from others who are unable to understand the complexity of this situation. Many of them have heard all the advice to try harder, reduce stress, and think positively, but they have become exhausted from trying every possible strategy.

It is an implied thought process that if you manage stress better, you will feel better. This thought completely misses reality because, even though you do everything right, you can still have a terrible day. This is a reality of living with chronic illness.

Meditation, prayer, eating well, and exercise within your limits can still leave you waking up in pain. Christian counselors, who are trained to work with individuals who struggle with chronic illnesses, understand that managing stress does not cure the condition. The goal of managing stress is to help you cope with something that isn’t going away. This goal is not to be seen as failure, but instead as wisdom.

Cast all your anxiety on him because he cares for you. – 1 Peter 5:7, NIV

Finding Rest It Doesn’t Bring Healing

Healthy people rest to recover. They always feel better after sleeping off a cold or taking a day off to recharge. But you feel as though you could rest for days, weeks, or months and still wake up sick and unrestored because there’s nothing temporary to recover from.

Frustration builds as you follow all the recommendations, trying to pace yourself and saying no to commitments, and your body still does not cooperate. The fatigue remains, and the pain persists, leading you to question whether rest even matters because it never leads to healing.

Even though rest does not offer a cure, it still has value. The value is in the difference between barely surviving and having small reserves for what matters. This is the space where you hear God’s voice rather than the demands of your body. It’s recognizing that biblical rest isn’t about earning healing through proper behavior. It is about accepting the limitations and trusting God with them.

The Sabbath was never meant to be conditional on your productivity or on whether it will make you feel better. Rest has always been an act of faith that acknowledges your worth doesn’t depend on what your body can accomplish.

For those with a chronic illness, this perspective can help them shift from a failed strategy to a spiritual practice. You began to understand you’re not resting to fix yourself. You are resting because you are human and your body needs compassion.

He makes me lie down in green pastures, he leads me beside quiet waters, he refreshes my soul. – Psalm 23:2-3a, NIV

Managing Stress Through Faith and Community

Isolation intensifies stress. When you’re sick, it is easy to withdraw from others because socializing takes energy you don’t have. Few people will understand what you’re going through. You have grown tired of explaining, so you rarely mention how you feel because it is often minimized or met with unhelpful solutions.

It’s understandable why isolation seems like the answer; however, isolation creates its own problems. Without connection, the stress becomes overwhelming. You end up losing perspective, and your world shrinks to just you and your symptoms.

Faith communities should be places where people with chronic illnesses can find support. However, this is not always the case, because church can sometimes feel like another place where you’re expected to perform and show up with a smile, regardless of your limitations. Christian counselors can help you navigate this situation by identifying truly supportive relationships and letting go of those that demand more than they will give.

In the Bible, the model of community is not about everyone being strong and capable all the time. It is a model of the body of Christ functioning together with different people contributing what they can and receiving what they need. In this community, you do not have to earn your place by being useful; your presence matters even when you can’t serve on committees or volunteer in ministries.

Finding or creating a community that understands your situation requires being intentional about who you connect with. This could mean joining a chronic illness support group or being honest with a few trusted friends about what you need. Managing stress isn’t a solo journey. Social support can significantly impact stress levels and health outcomes when you find people who can sit with you in your uncertainty and not try to fix it.

Carry each other’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ. – Galatians 6:2, NIV

Moving Forward with Chronic Illness

You don’t have to accept battles that don’t end with victory when you live with chronic illness. You don’t have to conquer your condition or will yourself into wellness to manage stress. Living with a chronic illness means that you make peace with the reality you didn’t choose while you refuse to let that reality define your entire existence.

The journey toward peace with chronic illness isn’t a straight path, and there is no timeline for when you should feel better. With the proper support, faith, and self-compassion, the stress will become something you can live with rather than something that consumes you. A Christian counselor can help you navigate this. Connect with a counselor near you or on this site to learn more.

item.title: How Thought Distortions Affect Relationships and What You Can Do About Them
item.description:
There’s a good chance that misunderstandings and wrong beliefs are causing many struggles you might be having in your relationship, you have about yourself, your partner, and other people. It’s common for people to have a biased way of thinking without even realizing that they are in the wrong.

It’s only when someone shows them with practical examples that they can begin to realize how skewed their beliefs have been. These misconceptions and incorrect beliefs are called thought distortions, and they are behind many of the issues people have in relationships.

A thought distortion is like a lens on a camera. When placed on a camera, a lens will distort or enhance reality in different ways, making everything seem broader, darker, or exaggerating small details to seem enormous. Similarly, sometimes people see the world through a lens that distorts reality.

They see the ordinary things others see as malicious and hurtful, and they focus on minor issues until they become big deals while ignoring other information. When you understand which lens or thought distortion you are viewing the world through, you can begin to challenge your point of view and change the way you think about yourself and your loved ones.

Examples of Thought Distortions

There is a small list of thought distortions, and each one has been named. This is to make it easier to identify and label the exact thought distortion you have been affected by, so that you can begin challenging it. You may have been viewing life through multiple lenses, but it is also possible to identify and challenge each one.

Perhaps you draw broad conclusions about people based on one interaction. Let’s say that your partner forgot about your birthday, and you concluded that they no longer care about you or the relationship anymore. This is called overgeneralization, and it causes you to come to unfair and untrue conclusions about others.

Over time, overgeneralization will cause your partner to feel constantly judged and mistrusted by you, because their small mistakes have an intense effect on you. If you frequently come to the worst conclusions about your partner’s actions, you could be affected by overgeneralization.

Similar to overgeneralization is personalization. Rather than making assumptions about your partner’s behavior, though, this is when you take too much responsibility for your own behavior. You regularly assume that you have done something wrong, even when there isn’t a problem.

Your partner might be quiet because they are decompressing from a stressful day, but you assume that they are quiet because you did something to upset them. As with many of the other thought distortions, personalization will cause you to become defensive even when nothing is wrong, and you will feel attacked even when receiving balanced feedback.

One of the most common thought distortions in relationships is mind-reading. This is exactly what it sounds like: you form conclusions about your partner and your relationship without even checking in with them or asking questions.

You assume that they have lost interest in you because they have become slower at responding to texts, or you believe that they are lying when they say they are not in a bad mood. Besides being frustrating and disrespectful to your partner, mind-reading will cause you to withdraw and feel resentful even when there is no real issue.

Emotional reasoning often goes hand in hand with mind-reading. This is when you treat your feelings as if they are facts. Examples of this are “I am anxious, so that must mean they are pulling away from me” or “I feel numb, so that means I have lost interest in the relationship.” When you make decisions based on your emotions, it is impulsive and will lead you to unfairly accuse your partner, threaten them, or become clingy and insecure.

Alongside emotional reasoning is catastrophic thinking. This is when you blow events out of proportion and expect the worst outcome from them. One fight can feel like the end of the relationship, or a perceived flirtatious remark to a stranger could lead you to assume that your partner wants to be unfaithful. This increases anxiety and causes you to constantly seek reassurance or stay on the offensive with your partner.

Often, these thoughts have a significant impact on your relationship. It’s important to remember that your relationship is a lot stronger than you are giving it credit for.

Challenging Thought Distortions

There are many other thought distortions, and it helps to become aware of them. The first step in challenging and overcoming them is knowing what they are in the first place. At any point in your relationship, you can self-reflect on an incident and ask yourself if you might have had a lens over your thinking. If so, identify which thought distortion you were viewing it through.

It helps to keep a journal, whether physical or digital, to track your thoughts in real time. You can be as detailed or minimal as you like, but record things like the situation, the emotion you felt in that moment, and your corresponding thoughts about it.

For example, you could write down that you argued with your partner, that you felt afraid in that moment, and that your corresponding thought was that they are planning on leaving you. You have identified the emotion you felt in the moment and can deduce that you were looking at the event through the distorted lens of emotional reasoning. Keeping a written record like this will help you see your blind spots and root out any thought distortions.

Keeping a journal is just the start of the self-reflection work you must do to challenge these thought distortions. The real work begins when you begin considering alternative thoughts in relation to the events in your relationship. Using the previous example in the journal, if you had an argument with your partner and you felt anxious that they were going to leave you, you could ask the following questions as a challenge to your thoughts:

  • Do you have any evidence that they are planning on leaving you?
  • What can you do to feel more secure in the relationship?
  • Is there evidence that proves the opposite? In other words, is there evidence that your partner wants to stay with you?

When you can name the thought distortion and the emotion surrounding it, you can begin challenging it with structured questions like these. When you do this regularly, you will find a new perspective on events in your life and gather evidence that contradicts your thoughts and emotions.

This can be an uncomfortable process because you are changing your mental and emotional foundations. This is necessary both for your mental health and for the long-term health of your relationship.

You’re not a bad person for having thought distortions. They are common, but they are also damaging. To grow as an individual and to become a better partner, you must understand which lens you are viewing the world through and begin the process of removing it from your thinking.

Feelings are not facts, but they do help you understand more about yourself and your loved ones. Regardless of what happened in the past, you can still grow, mature, and save your relationship.

Support on Your Journey

Growing and changing is not easy to do alone, and it helps to have someone else to give their perspective on your struggles. This is why people go for counseling; it helps to have an informed, neutral third party to offer their insight and prompt you to figure things out for yourself.

If you would like to find a counselor, you can start by checking out the online catalog of counselors on this website. You may also speak with the reception team, who will be happy to help you find someone who can support you on your journey to challenge thought distortions in your life. Connect with the team today.

item.title: Refilling Your Cup: Self-Care for Moms
item.description:
It’s an old but powerful adage that you can’t pour out from an empty cup. You simply cannot give to others something that you yourself do not possess. Moms often have full days that require a lot from them: mediating disputes, making a dollar stretch as far as possible, feeding others and nurturing their bodies and souls, teaching, and more. Self-care for moms isn’t really an option. It’s necessary if they want to keep doing their job well.

Why Moms Need Self-Care

The call to mothering is a profound and challenging one. Nurturing another human being, whether they are a baby, toddler, teen, or adult, isn’t easy, and it can often be exhausting. For some moms, that nurturing role is combined with a career or day job that splits their attention and needs them to juggle things to make it all work. Self-sacrifice at work and at home becomes the daily reality.

Moms get so many messages, whether from the world or from the church, about who they are or who they are supposed to be. One message is that putting yourself on the line and sacrificing yourself entirely for your children is a virtue and the highest form of love. The typical result of such messaging is that mothers run themselves ragged trying to keep up with the relentless pace and needs from every corner.

There is an invisible weight to motherhood that is hard to explain to others. As a mom tries to carry that weight, she might find herself feeling depleted, and she can’t give to other people when her own reserves are tapped out. Caring for yourself as a mom isn’t an indulgence, but an essential part of life. There really isn’t another way for you to sustain the presence and love your family requires from you without that self-care.

In Proverbs 31, there’s a verse that says, “She is clothed with strength and dignity; she can laugh at the days to come.” (Proverbs 31:25, NIV) That is a goal worth aspiring to for a mom or anyone else, but it requires taking time. You need to replenish your reserves, recalibrate, and reconnect with the Lord as you journey deeper into His purposes for your life. In other words, it requires some self-care.

Moms need self-care because the benefits of that care ripple outward to the people around them. When you care for yourself, you’re more emotionally regulated, more joyful, more present, more patient, and better able to handle difficulty. Taking care of yourself also serves as a powerful model for your kids that a person’s needs matter. When you care for yourself, you guard yourself against resentment as well as burnout, which can creep in over time.

Defining Self-Care

Self-care is the cluster of habits and practices that you engage in to attend to your own emotional, mental, physical, and spiritual needs. These habits and practices help you to sustain your capacity to love and live well. They are intentional, and when they are used consistently, these practices and habits help you to show up as the person, mother, and partner that you want to be.

The habits and practices that make up self-care don’t all look the same for every mother. That’s because each mother is unique, as are her circumstances, personality, resources, support networks, and relationships. Taking self-care seriously doesn’t necessarily mean having hours of uninterrupted time every day, week, or month. That would be wonderful if you could get it, but life doesn’t always work that way.

Assuming that self-care requires a huge time investment could serve as a barrier preventing you from trying. It’s more practical to think of it as something that can be pursued in a mom’s daily rhythms. It is something to be found in small moments, and the longer-term investments you make into your own flourishing.

Self-Care for Moms – Some Practices and Habits to Consider

Self-care is often one of the first things to go when life gets hectic, and it sometimes doesn’t even make it on the priority list. However, taking care of yourself is what allows you to show up effectively for others. Think about how much better you are at carrying the mantle of mom when you’ve had a good night’s rest compared to when you got a smattering of sleep, if that. You’re more patient, present, and creative when you’re well rested.

As you think about your own self-care routine, consider the shape of your life, the resources you have on hand, and the demands on your time and capacity. Self-care when you have young children and are recently back in the workforce won’t necessarily look the same five years later. Below are a few daily self-care practices you can consider adopting, as well as some long-term strategies you can use for ongoing wellness.

Eat well and drink water This is quite basic, but moms can neglect doing the basics because life gets busy, and their focus is on taking care of everyone else. Take the time to eat regular, nourishing meals as part of your self-care. Doing so fuels your body and also allows you to skirt the possibility of being hangry (anger that comes from hunger).

Have quiet mornings Taking even fifteen minutes for yourself before your household wakes up can help set a great tone for your day. It’s the sort of thing you can and should communicate to your family so that you have that time to yourself. You can use it to pray, read Scripture, or simply sit in silence with a nice cup of tea.

Move your body Movement helps to elevate your mood, reduce your stress levels, and reconnect with your own body. Movement can take the form of gentle stretches, a short walk, riding a bike, dancing, or Pilates. As long as it gets you moving, it works.

Connect with other adults One of the dangers for moms is becoming isolated and not having someone with whom to have grown-up conversations. A mom needs to connect with other adults. Call your mom, grab a coffee with a friend, or have conversations with your partner. Having relationships that go beyond your children is a must.

Name your feelings Being a mom brings complex emotional experiences with it. Part of self-care is orienting yourself and knowing what you feel. Allow yourself to name those feelings and experiences, whether it’s joy, grief, frustration, or loneliness. The aim isn’t to judge yourself, but to own your emotions and understand your own thoughts and feelings so they don’t catch you off guard.

Take in beauty Gratitude and the ability to see beauty are powerful weapons that can help you regulate your mood better. Make it a habit to try to notice something beautiful every day. It could be a piece of music, the colors of the evening sky, a child’s laugh, or a line from a poem or song. When reading the Psalms, like Psalm 19 and 104, you can pick up examples of attentiveness to beauty and God’s creation.

Regular respite Where possible, even if it’s brief, build in regular time during your day, week, or month away from parenting responsibilities. You’re not abandoning your children or your responsibilities; you’re taking time away to replenish yourself.

Carve out something of your own Pursue something of your own, whether it’s a creative practice like art, a hobby, or an area of learning and growth that doesn’t have anything to do with your role as a mom. Being Mom is a part of who you are, but it is not the entirety of your identity, and it’s important to keep that awareness.

Have honest friendships Along similar lines, it’s important that you have other mothers or women who know you well. These are people with whom you can be honest and raw about the messy and difficult parts of being a mom without being performative and without needing to maintain illusions.

Counseling or therapy Counseling isn’t only for when it feels like life is falling apart. Even in those spaces and times when things are manageable, counseling offers you a space to reflect on your inner life so that you know how you are doing. Counseling offers you a safe space to process the various losses, demands, joys, and complexities of motherhood.

Your counselor is someone who will listen to you without judgment, and they are positioned to help you grow as you identify concerns and develop the tools to handle those challenges effectively. Prioritizing your own well-being matters for the reasons noted earlier. If you would like support in building a balanced life where your needs are also addressed, contact our reception team to get started on that journey.

item.title: Pet Grief in Older Adults: Finding Comfort Through Faith
item.description:
The loss of a pet is devastating at any age, but for older adults, the grief can carry a weight that is hard to understand. After decades of life experiences, most people seem to think that older adults have developed the ability to face grief more easily than the rest of us. The reality is more complex.

When an older adult loses a pet that has been part of their daily lives for many years, they can feel overwhelmed by the grief. If a pet has been their constant companion through retirement, illness, or the loss of a spouse, this loss can be painful and lonely. The good news is that this pain can be an opportunity to lean into the grace of God and know how His comfort will extend to their heart.

The Lord is close to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit. – Psalm 34:18, NIV

Understanding the Depth of Pet Grief in Older Adults

Culture tells us that some losses aren’t that important. For older adults, this message creates a hard situation when they are devastated by the loss of a pet and question the legitimacy of their pain. Pet loss is often dismissed as something that should be sad but easy to get over. This reflects a deeper assumption about aging and emotional resilience that keeps older adults disconnected from their unique emotional experiences.

Many older adults have connections with their pets that go beyond companionship. Their pets have become part of their daily routine and the reason they get up each morning. Some adults have no one else in their lives, so their furry friends have become the only one who depends on them.

When there are no adult children nearby, and a spouse has passed away, a pet will fill the void and go beyond friendship. These loving pets will create a purpose and show unconditional love. This will create a sense of being needed for the older adult who is now the caregiver for this living creature.

The grief of pet loss can often mimic that of human relationships. The shock of the silence when there is no barking or purring that once resonated creates a lonely silence for the owner. There may be feelings of guilt due to decisions regarding life-ending care. Anger is common as the world continues to be okay, while the pet owner feels devastated. The contradiction of these feelings creates a sense of falling apart, even though they look fine to those around them.

Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted. – Matthew 5:4, NIV

When Grief Feels Overwhelming and Isolating

Pet grief in older adults is often accompanied by isolation. This isolation is a response to well-meaning suggestions that seem hurtful to those who have lost their companion. Some family and friends may suggest getting another pet, but this doesn’t negate the pain they feel about the unique pet they just lost.

These suggestions can create a sense of emotional isolation because others don’t understand how special their pet was. While people often mean well, this message conveys that the pain isn’t worthy of respect. The dismissive attitude of this mindset creates a hidden burden for older adults who are already struggling with multiple losses and health challenges.

The pet that was by their side daily and provided emotional support during difficult times is no longer present, and the grief is being compounded by the feeling that the grief should be hidden. Some older adults feel embarrassed about the depth of their grief and end up isolating themselves and navigating the grieving process in silence.

The practical aspect adds another layer of complexity. The bills for veterinary care, cremation costs, and the physical demands of caring for an ill pet bring with them a level of stress that goes beyond the emotional pain. Adults with fixed incomes or limited mobility often feel like these challenges are impossible to overcome, creating a tangled web of feelings of helplessness, regret, and grief.

Christian counselors understand that this type of complicated grief requires a gentle process. They recognize that the shame associated with pet loss is often the reason older adults dismiss the thought of getting support. As a result, a generation of older adults feels they must process loss and dismiss validation.

Even though I walk through the darkest valley, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me. – Psalm 23:4, NIV

Finding Comfort in Faith During Pet Loss

Faith can offer a unique perspective on pet loss and be a profound comfort during the grieving process. The God who created every creature with purpose and love understands the bonds that older adults form with their companions.

Scripture doesn’t minimize these relationships but rather points to a Creator who values all of His creation. This understanding can encourage older adults to find peace in knowing their grief is acknowledged by a Father who understands.

Prayer can be a powerful tool for processing the complex emotions of pet loss. Unlike human relationships that can come with complications and unfinished business, relationships with pets often represent pure love and acceptance. When this kind of pain is brought to God in prayer, the outcome is an honest expression of loss without the need to justify your feelings to those who may not understand.

It often helps older adults view their role as pet caregivers through a spiritual lens. When a person takes on the responsibility of caring for another living being of God’s creation and shows compassion during illness, it reflects Christian love in action. This is a transformative perspective that can turn feelings of guilt or regret into a recognition of faithful stewardship.

Christian counselors often assist with this situation by encouraging the exploration of faith and its relationship with loss and grief. This process involves acknowledging that love creates vulnerability to pain, but that pain is not meaningless in suffering. In times of loss, the pain becomes an opportunity to experience God’s comfort in new depths. This helps us understand how He connects with us during our grieving process.

Praise be to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort those who are in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves receive from God. – 2 Corinthians 1:3-4, NIV

Moving Forward with Hope and Healing

Healing from pet loss doesn’t mean forgetting or minimizing the relationship that was lost. Rather, it involves learning to carry the love and memories forward while allowing space for life to continue. The process often requires patience and recognizing that grief has no predetermined timeline or proper way to unfold.

Some practical steps can help older adults process the grief of losing their furry loved one. By doing these things, grief can be transformed into a special remembrance that can help provide closure for the loss of the relationship. A few ideas are:

  • Plant a garden
  • Create a photo album
  • Donate to an animal shelter
  • Create a memorial space for the pet

Faith communities can also support older adults through pet grief. If a church acknowledges that these losses are just as important as other losses that people experience, then that church community is validating the pain and creating a network of support. There have been some instances of churches finding meaningful ways to honor the role of pets through blessing ceremonies or memorial services.

Christian counselors emphasize that moving forward after pet loss doesn’t mean immediate action or decisions about future pets. The focus is on processing the current loss and allowing God’s comfort to work through the natural grieving process. Some older adults may find peace in opening their hearts to another pet companion, while others feel they need to follow a different healing path.

The journey through pet loss grief can ultimately deepen faith and the understanding of God’s compassion. Many times, these older adults feel closer to God after walking through a hard season of loss through tangibly experiencing His comfort.

“For I know the plans I have for you,” declares the LORD, “plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future.” – Jeremiah 29:11, NIV

Consider Support

Pet grief in older adults reflects a depth of love and connection, demonstrating the capacity for relationship and care. Faith offers comfort and a fresh perspective, allowing older adults to honor their grief and love, finding solace in God’s promise of comfort.

Christian counselors can help them navigate pain through understanding what God says about grief. This allows for a more natural healing process rather than one that is hidden because the loss is culturally less important.
